subject: Climate & Environment
title: Attribution Science
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Attribution Science.

hook.text: Can we blame a single storm on climate change? A new science says yes — with numbers.

buildup.text: Attribution science compares what happened to what would have happened without human warming.

discovery.text: Scientists run climate models with and without added CO₂, then compare the probability of events.

twist.text: The 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave was found to be virtually impossible without climate change.

climax.text: Attribution studies now take days instead of months — fast enough to inform disaster response.

punchline.text: We can now put a number on how much climate change loaded the dice.

quiz.question: What does attribution science determine?
options: How much climate change influenced a specific weather event
Which country caused the most emissions
When the next storm will happen

details.summary: Attribution science determines how much climate change contributed to a specific extreme weather event by comparing observed conditions to simulated worlds without human emissions. It has shown that many recent heat waves, floods, and droughts were made significantly worse by warming.
details.whyItMatters: Attribution science answers the question people ask after every disaster: was this caused by climate change? Its findings are increasingly used in legal cases and policy debates.
takeaways: Rapid attribution studies can be completed within days of an event
The 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome was virtually impossible without warming
Attribution results are being used in climate litigation worldwide

faq.question: How does attribution science work?
faq.answer: Scientists run climate models of the actual world and a hypothetical world without human greenhouse gas emissions. By comparing event likelihood in both scenarios, they calculate how much human influence increased the probability or intensity of the event.

faq.question: Has attribution science been used in court?
faq.answer: Yes. Attribution findings have been cited in lawsuits against fossil fuel companies and governments. The science provides evidence linking specific climate damages to specific emissions, supporting legal arguments for liability and compensation.
